Published on 31st August 2026, Updated for 2027 — stay ahead of the UX calendar and pick the right event for your growth and networking.

As the UX & product design landscape keeps shifting — with AI-native workflows, research maturity, service design and cross-discipline collaboration all competing for a seat at the table — picking the right conference can sharpen your craft, grow your network, and reset your thinking for the year ahead. Below are the UX / UX-adjacent events worth planning around for 2027. Several 2027 editions haven't locked exact dates yet at time of writing (organizers typically confirm 4-6 months out) — we've flagged those clearly, and we'll keep this page updated as details land. (As always, double-check the event website before booking travel.)

## Top UX Conferences to attend in 2027

### 1. ACM IUI 2027 (32nd Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces)

Dates: 8-11 February 2027 Venue: Helsinki Congress Paasitorni, Helsinki, Finland Focus: The premier academic venue sitting at the intersection of AI and human-computer interaction — interactive machine learning, generative interfaces, human-in-the-loop AI, and explainability. Why consider it: If your UXR work increasingly touches AI-driven or adaptive interfaces, IUI is where the research a year or two ahead of shipped product gets presented first. Link: ACM IUI 2027

### 2. prompt:UX Berlin 2027

Dates: 24-25 February 2027 (conference + optional full-day workshop) Venue: Hotel AMANO Eastside, Berlin, Germany Focus: Europe's dedicated conference on the intersection of AI and UX design — case studies and hands-on workshops for designers, researchers and product managers. Why consider it: A tight, practitioner-focused (not academic) look at how AI is actually changing day-to-day UX work, with an early-in-the-year timing that sets the tone for the rest of your conference calendar. Link: prompt:UX Berlin 2027

### 3. ConveyUX 2027

Dates: February 2027 (exact dates to be announced) Venue: Seattle, US, and virtual Focus: A long-running Seattle conference covering accessibility, design, strategy and AI across multiple tracks, with both in-person and virtual options. Why consider it: Strong practitioner lineup, accessible pricing relative to the big US conferences, and a track record of staying current on AI-in-UX topics. Link: ConveyUX

### 4. ACM CHI 2027

Dates: 10-14 May 2027 Venue: David L. Lawrence Convention Center, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA Focus: The flagship international HCI research conference — this year's theme, "Bridges," spans papers, panels, workshops and a strong applied-AI research track given the Carnegie Mellon-based general chairs. Why consider it: Still the must-attend for anyone doing UX research who wants to stay current with HCI theory, methods, and where academic research is heading next. Link: CHI 2027

### 5. UX London 2027

Dates: Typically early June (2027 dates not yet announced) Venue: London, UK Focus: Organized by Clearleft — three days, each pairing a morning of talks with an afternoon of hands-on workshops across research, product, interface design, content strategy and design systems. Why consider it: One of the best UK options if travel budget or visas make the US conferences harder to justify. Link: UX London

### 6. Figma Config 2027

Dates: Typically late June (2027 dates not yet announced; 2026 ran 23-25 June) Venue: Moscone Center, San Francisco, US, plus free virtual access Focus: Figma's flagship conference — design, product development and AI-in-tooling from design leaders, plus first looks at Figma's own roadmap. Why consider it: Even if you're tool-agnostic, Config has become a genuine bellwether for where design tooling and AI-assisted workflows are heading. Link: Figma Config

### 7. IDC 2027 (Interaction Design and Children)

Dates: 21-24 June 2027 Venue: Seattle, Washington, USA Focus: A specialized HCI conference on design, interaction and technology for children — this year's tracks include AI literacy, safety, and education. Why consider it: Directly relevant if your UX domain touches children, education, family products, or inclusive design more broadly. Link: IDC 2027

### 8. HCI International 2027

Dates: 25-30 July 2027 Venue: Estrel Hotel and Congress Center, Berlin, Germany (with online participation) Focus: A week-long, multi-theme HCI academic conference with dozens of affiliated tracks — AI-HCI, human-robot interaction, mobility/automotive HCI, and more. Why consider it: Best pick if you want breadth and depth in one trip, and are comfortable with an academic-conference format and pace. Link: HCI International 2027

### 9. INTERACT 2027

### Dates: 23-27 August 2027 Venue: Tallinn, Estonia Focus: The 21st IFIP TC13 International Conference on Human-Computer Interaction, themed "Meanings and Experiences" — drawing on Estonian semiotician Juri Lotman's cultural semiotics to explore how meaning is shaped through interaction, alongside the usual full-paper, short-paper, panel, course and doctoral-consortium tracks. Why consider it: One of the longest-running international HCI research conferences (IFIP-sponsored, not ACM), and a genuinely different angle — semiotics and cultural meaning-making — for researchers who want more than the usual AI-and-interfaces framing. Link: INTERACT 2027

### 10. India HCI 2027

Dates: TBD (the conference has run every October/November for the last several editions; the 17th edition was hosted by IIT Hyderabad in October 2026) Venue: India — host institution rotates each year Focus: India's academic-practitioner HCI/UX conference series, run by HCIPAI — accessibility, user modelling, interactive systems and emerging tech. Why consider it: The regionally-important forum if you're based in India or the wider APAC UX community and want a conference closer to home. Link: India HCI / HCIPAI

### ✅ How to Pick the Right Conference for You

- Define your goal: Are you upskilling in design/UX craft, broadening your network, going deep on research methods, or building cross-functional relationships with product and engineering?

- Budget & travel: Weigh Europe vs. US, in-person vs. hybrid/online, and how far in advance you can lock in early-bird pricing.

- Format & size: Some of these are 5,000+ person spectacles (Config, CHI); others are deliberately small and sponsor-free (UX Nordic, UXinsight). Decide what actually helps you learn.

- Specific focus: Research-centric (UXinsight, CHI, HCII), tool-centric (Config), cross-functional (UXDX), or broadly UX/design/product (UXLx, UX London)?

- Timing within your year: Front-load with an early-year event like IUI or prompt:UX for fresh thinking, and use a Q3/Q4 pick like uxcon vienna or Future Product Days to reset before planning season.

### 🔍 Final Thoughts

2027 is shaping up to be another AI-saturated year for UX and product design conferences — nearly every major event on this list now runs an explicit AI/human-AI interaction track, whether that's IUI's computational-innovation theme, CHI's applied-AI research strand out of Pittsburgh, or Config's AI-workflow focus. Several 2027 dates are still to be confirmed at time of writing; we'll update this article as organizers lock venues and pricing, so bookmark it and check back before you commit travel budget.

TL;DR: UX research for AI products works best as a four-phase loop, the AI-native research lifecycle: Discover where AI is worth building, Define what "good" means, Evaluate the AI against real people, and Monitor trust after launch. Each phase hands the next one something it needs, which is why researchers belong in every phase and not only in testing.

Who this is for: UX researchers, product designers and product managers building AI features, assistants or agents.

Every AI team has a meeting where someone says, "The model scored really well. Are we good to ship?" Nobody in the room can fully answer. The score came from a benchmark, the benchmark came from the team's own guesses about what users ask, and no real user has touched any of it yet.

That gap is where researchers belong. I'd go further: of all the roles on an AI product team, ours is the one that can speak for the person on the other end of the prompt, at every step of the build, not only the last one.

## What is the AI product lifecycle?

In classic software, you design, build, test, ship, and then mostly move on. AI products don't work that way. The thing you ship is probabilistic, the quality bar is a judgement call, and the behaviour keeps changing after launch because models, data and user habits keep changing. So the life of an AI product is a loop with four moves:

- Discover : decide where AI is worth building at all.

- Define : say precisely what "good" looks like.

- Evaluate : check whether the AI clears that bar, according to real people.

- Monitor : keep listening once it is live.

## Why is UX research central to AI product development?

Each of those four moves hinges on a human question that no dashboard can answer for you. Where does work really hurt? Whose idea of a good answer counts? Do users accept what the model produced? Is their trust going up or down? Those are research questions. If researchers only show up at usability testing, the team has already made the big calls on instinct.

This is the framework I use to stay involved from the first idea to the long tail after launch. It gives you a clear role at every stage, a named set of methods you already know, and one thread running through it all: build it with the people who will use it. Each phase also produces something the next phase cannot start without, which is what turns four activities into one story.

Read it clockwise. Whatever you learn at the end of the loop goes straight back to the start.

## Phase 1: Discover. How do you find where AI is worth building?

In short: Discover is the first phase of the AI-native research lifecycle. Researchers map real workflows, combine behavioural data with fieldwork, and run an AI opportunity workshop to find friction worth solving. The output is a prioritized AI opportunity map that shows the team where AI will genuinely help.

Most AI projects start with a technology and go looking for a problem. Discovery flips that. Your job is to find the places where people lose time, switch tools, repeat themselves or hold things in their head, and then ask honestly whether AI would help.

### Your role as the researcher

You are the person who sees the whole workflow, not just the screen the team owns. Start with a signal, usually from data science: a lot of people hopping between two tools, a task that takes far longer than it should. Then make "is this a real problem, and why?" the research question. Name the riskiest assumption and test it with people before anyone gets excited.

### Methods I reach for

- Journey mapping across the full toolchain, to see where effort piles up.

- Behavioural log analysis , with a data scientist, to find where people switch, repeat or drop off.

- In-product micro-surveys (a short CSAT-style pulse) to see how widely the pain is felt.

- Contextual inquiry and job shadowing , to watch the workaround happen and hear the reason for it.

- Non-obvious sources when the obvious data is silent: internal forum threads, support tickets, hand-coded with thematic analysis .

- An AI opportunity workshop with product, design and engineering: map roles and workflows, plot frequency against impact, and separate "existing but faster" from "AI-first" ideas.

The design underneath is explanatory sequential mixed methods . The numbers tell you what is happening, the fieldwork tells you why, and you check both in one shared findings document so nobody argues from half the picture.

### Who to bring along

A data scientist from day one, because the signal is theirs and the explanation is yours. Then the PM, a designer and a couple of engineers for the workshop, plus the people who do the work every day. Engineers in the room keep the list honest about what is feasible.

### What you hand to the next phase

A prioritized AI opportunity map: each opportunity scored on severity, frequency and how suited it is to AI, with an owner and an evidence trail behind it. This is the raw material for Define. Without it, Define has nothing real to write prompts about.

### Mistakes to avoid

- Starting from "we need AI" instead of a friction in someone's day.

- Believing the log signal without asking why. The data shows what, not why.

- Running the workshop with partners but no end users, so the ideas are impressive and unwanted.

- Counting identified waste as saved effort. Until something ships, it is only an estimate.

- Ranking opportunities with no owner, so the map becomes a poster.

## Phase 2: Define. How do you decide what a good AI answer looks like?

In short: Define turns a chosen opportunity into something testable. Researchers crowdsource real prompts from expert users, agree a rubric, and run co-creation workshops to write expected answers. The output is a prompt set, a rubric and a golden dataset that the AI will be measured against.

Discover gave you an opportunity. Define turns it into something a team can build against and test. In practice that means three things: real prompts, a shared rubric, and a set of expected answers, often called a golden dataset. Here is the part I care about most as a researcher: whoever writes those expected answers is setting the standard the model will be judged by for the rest of its life. That is enormous influence, and it should not sit with whoever happens to be closest to the code.

You make sure "good" is defined by users, not guessed by the team. You collect the questions people truly ask, help the group agree which ones matter most, and sit people with real expertise in a room to describe what a great answer looks like.

- Prompt crowdsourcing from expert segments, so the test set uses the language people really use.

- Collaborative scoring of each prompt on severity, frequency and importance, with the scale agreed up front.

- Participatory design and co-creation workshops : users, product and engineering in one room, everyone drafts the expected response, the room reviews, engineers size feasibility live.

- Rubric design with clear anchor descriptions for each score, in the spirit of behaviourally anchored rating scales.

- Inter-rater agreement checks on the expected answers, to see where experts truly differ.

Expect more than one acceptable answer for many prompts. Capturing those variations is not messy, it is accurate. A single "right" answer will later mark good responses as failures.

The expert users whose judgement defines quality, plus engineering and design. Add a data scientist to check that the prompt set reflects the real spread of use, not just the loudest cases.

A prioritized prompt set, a plain-language rubric, and a golden dataset with approved responses and accepted variations. Engineering gets a head start on building. Evaluate gets something concrete to test against. Nothing in the next phase works without these.

- Writing prompts in the team's own vocabulary, so the AI is tested on questions nobody asks.

- Using novice raters to define ground truth in an expert domain.

- Keeping the rubric vague, so every score becomes an argument.

- Treating the golden dataset as finished. It ages as the product and users change.

## Phase 3: Evaluate. How do you know an AI product is good enough to ship?

In short: Evaluate tests whether the AI is good enough according to real users. Researchers compare human-as-judge and LLM-as-judge scores, study where they disagree (the judge gap), and turn rejection reasons into fixes. The output is a launch-readiness view and a repeatable evaluation step.

Now you have prompts, a rubric and expected answers, so you can finally ask whether the AI is good enough. Most teams answer with an automated judge: another model that scores the output. That is fast and cheap, and it can also be confidently wrong. The researcher's move here is simple and powerful: put human judgement beside the automated score and study the gap between them.

I have seen an automated judge report that a feature was nearly ready while real users, rating the same outputs, accepted far fewer of them. The headline number was not lying on purpose. It was measuring something slightly different from what users care about. Finding that out before launch is one of the most valuable things a researcher can do.

You are the check on the checker. You compare human-as-judge and LLM-as-judge results, work out where and why they diverge, and turn user rejections into specific things engineering can fix. You also agree the launch bar with the team before the results come in, so the goalposts stay put.

- Human-as-judge rating against the Define rubric, with trained expert raters.

- LLM-as-judge comparison , scored on the same prompts.

- Agreement analysis between the two (for example Cohen's kappa), cut by quality dimension and prompt type.

- An in-tool acceptance survey , so people judge real outputs in context.

- Thematic coding and affinity mapping of free-text rejection reasons, rolled up into structured factors.

- Error analysis : read the failures hiding inside a passing average.

- A second round after fixes, to confirm the gap actually narrowed.

The design here is convergent mixed methods : gather the acceptance signal and the rejection reasons side by side, then merge them. You need confidence quickly, from two angles.

The expert raters from Define, engineering and applied science who will act on the findings, and data science for the agreement statistics. Keep the people who built the automated judge close. They know where it is likely to fail.

A judge-gap readout, a ranked list of rejection factors with real examples, and a launch-readiness view against the agreed bar. You also leave behind a repeatable evaluation step the team can rerun after every model change. That step is what Monitor will keep running once the product is live.

- Trusting one accuracy number from an automated judge without checking it against people.

- Testing on prompts the model has already seen.

- Treating a pass mark as a verdict, when the failures sit inside the average.

- Reporting a thin sample as if it were precise. State the sample and the uncertainty.

- Moving the launch bar after seeing the results.

- Reporting the gap once and stopping. Measure again after each fix.

## Phase 4: Monitor. How do you track trust after launch?

In short: Monitor keeps trust measurable after launch. Researchers run a longitudinal in-product survey, track behavioural signals and re-run the evaluation set after every model change. The output is a trust trend, plus new failure cases and unmet needs that restart the loop.

Shipping is not the finish line for an AI product. Models get updated, data shifts, and people learn new ways to use the thing, so quality moves even when nobody touches the code. Monitoring is how you notice. As the researcher, you build the always-on listening that tells the team whether people trust the AI more or less than last month, and why.
